Key Insights & Recommendations

Synthesized findings and data-driven recommendations for product and user engagement strategies.

Activity Step Counts Are Broadly Healthy but Bimodal

The average daily step count of 10,574 steps surpasses the commonly cited 10,000-step benchmark on average. However, the distribution is broad (std ~5,400), with a meaningful segment of users recording under 5,800 steps/day. Running and Walking workouts correlate with the highest step tallies, while Yoga and Gym sessions produce lower totals — expected given their sedentary-vs-locomotion nature. Age groups 26–45 are the most active steppers.

Sleep Sleep Duration Is Adequate but Stress-Sensitive

The cohort averages 6.99 hours of sleep, close to the recommended 7–9 hour range. Critically, sleep duration shows a clear negative relationship with stress level: users at stress level 10 sleep noticeably less than those at level 1. Happy users sleep longer than Neutral and Tired users. This stress–sleep axis is one of the strongest behavioural signals in the dataset and warrants targeted product intervention.

Activity Workout Participation Sits at 83.1%

Roughly 83.1% of daily records include a structured workout session. Running is the most popular modality, followed by Yoga and Walking. Active workout days correlate with higher caloric burn, higher step counts, and — notably — greater water intake (~2.8 L vs ~2.3 L on rest days). Cycling sessions produce the highest average workout duration, suggesting a committed sub-segment of endurance users.

Lifestyle Stress & Mood Are Tightly Coupled

Stress level averages 5.45/10 across the cohort. The Tired mood category carries the highest average stress and lowest average step counts and sleep hours — forming a negative wellness triad. Happy users exhibit lower stress, more steps, and better sleep. Water intake does not significantly differ by mood, suggesting hydration is a baseline behaviour rather than a mood-driven one.

Product Weekday vs. Weekend Activity Differences Are Modest

Day-of-week analysis reveals no dramatic step-count cliff between weekdays and weekends, unlike real-world cohorts. Saturday and Sunday record slightly higher average steps than mid-week days, possibly reflecting leisure walks and longer outdoor workouts. This pattern is important for personalised notification timing — weekend morning nudges may be more effective than weekday evening reminders.

Product BMI Distribution Skews Healthy but Overweight Segment Is Substantial

Normal BMI users make up the plurality; the Overweight category is the second-largest. Obese users log lower average step counts and higher stress levels. Female users in this dataset have a marginally lower average BMI than Male users. Targeting the Overweight segment with incremental-activity challenges — rather than intensive workout prescriptions — is likely to yield the highest engagement lift per intervention unit.

Actionable Recommendations

1
Personalised Step Goals by Age & BMI

Replace one-size-fits-all step targets with adaptive goals calibrated to age group and BMI category. Users aged 46–60 and those in the Overweight/Obese segments should receive lower initial targets with progressive ramps to sustain motivation and reduce injury risk.

2
Stress-Triggered Sleep Coaching

Build a stress–sleep intervention flow: when a user reports or registers stress levels above 7, surface a sleep-hygiene micro-lesson and next-day recovery workout recommendation. The negative stress–sleep correlation in this data quantifies the business case for such a feature.

3
Workout Variety Challenges

Introduce monthly cross-modality challenges (e.g., "Try Yoga this week") for users whose workout_type is consistently single-category. The data shows that multi-type users tend to maintain higher step counts even on non-workout days, suggesting generalised habit carry-over.

4
Hydration Reminders on Workout Days

Active days see higher water intake, but baseline hydration (~2.5 L) is below recommended levels on rest days. Automated hydration nudges on non-workout days — particularly for high-stress users — could improve overall wellness scores and serve as a lightweight re-engagement touchpoint.

5
Mood-Aware Notification Timing

Integrate daily mood logs into the notification engine. Tired users should receive lower-intensity activity suggestions and early sleep reminders rather than high-step challenges. Happy users are the most responsive segment — use this window for premium feature promotions and social sharing nudges.

6
Seasonal Campaign Planning

Monthly step patterns show mid-year peaks. Plan engagement campaigns and new feature launches to coincide with the highest-activity months (Jun–Aug) to maximise adoption. Deploy re-engagement campaigns in lower-activity months (Jan–Feb) targeting lapsed users with low-barrier restart challenges.
